L’excellence noire : un fardeau pour cer: Black excellence: a burden for some members of the community
Un dialogue sur l’excellence noire et de: A dialogue on Black excellence and its impact on the mental health of young Black people.
« [La célébration de] l’excellence noire: “[Celebrating] Black excellence encourages you, but with a knife to your throat!” exclaims Manuel, a panellist at La Converse during an evening of dialogue on Black excellence and its impact on mental health.
Chaque année, durant le mois de février,: Every year in February, Canada and many other countries around the world celebrate Black History Month. The month is devoted to recognizing and celebrating the history of Black communities, and also to highlighting the achievements of some of their members. During this month, the hashtag #BlackExcellence, or in French #ExcellenceNoire, resurfaces in full force on social media. Although there is a glaring need for Black representation in the media, some see this celebration of Black excellence as a form of social pressure.
La Converse a souhaité accueillir dans s: La Converse invited Montrealers from Black communities to its offices to discuss the subject. Professionals and students alike, they begin a dialogue.
Nous sommes un mercredi soir, et l’espac: It’s a Wednesday evening, and La Converse’s studio space is welcoming its guests. Six panellists are present: Manuel, Adrianna, Nohémie, Lætitia, Paula and Anthony.
Manuel, l’aîné du groupe, est entreprene: Manuel, the eldest of the group, is an entrepreneur and human resources director at a private company. In his view, Black excellence is nothing less than a burden weighing on the community’s shoulders. “It takes away our right to make mistakes. Unlike others, who get to be good or bad without being dehumanized, we constantly have to do more to be accepted,” he says, as the people in the room nod in approval.
Nohémie est agente de programme au gouve: Nohémie is a government program officer and co-host of the radio show Ça vous choque ?, broadcast on CISM 89.3 FM. She argues that celebrating Black excellence obscures the challenges Black people face before they achieve success. “We often celebrate someone who made it in their neighbourhood, but we don’t talk about how their neighbourhood didn’t help them succeed – because of a lack of resources. We focus on that person and point out that they managed to stand out, when we should be making it possible for all the young people in the neighbourhood to stand out.”
Ces difficultés auxquelles font face les: The difficulties Black people face aren’t limited to the environment they grew up in, but extend to schools and workplaces as well, as our panellists remind us one after another.
<strong>« Il y a encore trop de “premier: “There are still too many ‘first Black people’”
Le rapport annuel de la Commission des d: The 2022 annual report of the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse indicates that only 11.2% of public-sector employees are members of visible minorities. However, no data specifies the exact percentage of Black employees.
Manuel, lui, constate que les Noirs sont: For his part, Manuel observes that Black people are still largely underrepresented in management positions in Quebec. “There are still too many ‘first Black people’ in the workplace,” he laments, as the others nod in agreement. “Many times, I’ve been the first Black manager, or even the only Black person at my job. In fact, diversity often starts with me,” he continues.
Manuel ressent le fardeau de représenter: Manuel feels the burden of representing his community with dignity so as not to jeopardize other Black people’s chances of landing positions like his. “Everything I do could close doors for the Black people who come after me. There’s no choice but to excel at work. I can’t just be Manu and focus solely on my career.”
Nohémie a éprouvé une pression similaire: Nohémie felt similar pressure when she founded the CÉRA (Comité des Étudiant.e.s Racisé.e.s de l’Association Étudiante de Science politique et Études internationales de l’Université de Montréal) in 2020. At first, she and three other classmates wanted to form a committee specifically for Black people. Faced with a “hostile environment,” she says, the co-founders ultimately took a more inclusive approach, offering a safe space for all racialized students.
« Il y avait une pression de devoir perf: “There was pressure to perform, because it was the first committee of its kind,” she explains. From the outset, the students had to deal with negative comments. “So we had no right to make mistakes,” she continues. “If it had failed, they could have shut the project down and never allowed a committee for racialized people again.” In less than two weeks, Nohémie and her team were burned out, she tells us.
<strong>« L’excellence noire, c’est auss: “Black excellence also means being the best model of integration”
La pression sociale exercée sur les indi: The social pressure placed on Black individuals isn’t limited to their professional performance; it also extends to their behaviour and personality, Lætitia, Manuel, Nohémie, Anthony and Paula tell us.
Lætitia, 20 ans, est étudiante en études: Lætitia, 20, is an international studies student at the Université de Montréal and an insurance agent. “People recognize the excellence of Black people, but only those who appeal to the Québécois public. Black excellence also means fitting the best model of integration,” she says.
La jeune femme reconnaît que, pour corre: The young woman acknowledges that, in order to fit this model and be better perceived, she gave up her freedom to choose how she dresses and wears her hair for a time. “I have traditional clothes, but I’m not going to wear a boubou to university, even though I think it’s really beautiful. As for my hair, even if it’s natural, it has to be slicked down with gel,” she explains.
Nohémie dit également ressentir une pres: Nohémie also says she feels constant pressure to look put-together. Unlike her colleagues, she doesn’t allow herself to be casual, even when working from home. “My colleagues have no problem telling me they’re in their pyjamas; me, I’m not going to tell them I’m in my pyjamas – no way!” she says, laughing. “My colleagues can swear, I can’t. I know there are certain things I can’t allow myself to do like the others, because it might be taken the wrong way. But no matter what I do or what I say, in the end, people will always see me as Black,” she concludes.
Manuel observe également une certaine re: Manuel also notes a certain restraint in his behaviour: “You have to be careful. You can’t be the ‘angry black man,’ you can’t lose it, you can’t have bad days either. You always have to be smiling, even when you’re exhausted.”
Anthony, consultant en science des donné: Anthony, a data science consultant, shares a different perspective. He says the pressure he felt wasn’t external, but rather self-imposed. Growing up, he sought to change how others saw him, especially because of his stutter as a child. “I walked crooked and I was the picture of the handicapped kid who could barely talk. Then I worked on myself, I started winning marathons and all kinds of awards. Every time I excel, I change how the people around me see me,” he says proudly.
<strong>« Quand tu es noir, tu commences: “When you’re Black, you start out in childhood with a high stress level, at 7 out of 10”
Le concept d’excellence noire va bien au: The concept of Black excellence goes well beyond mere outside pressure. For many, it takes root in childhood, at home, with pressure from parents. Some children are raised with the idea that they have to outdo themselves, that they have to do more than others if they hope to succeed one day.
« Quand tu es noir, tu commences dans l’: “When you’re Black, you start out in childhood with a high stress level, at 7 out of 10. Your parents teach you that you have to be twice as good,” Manuel replies. Nohémie responds with a knowing smile: “For my part, I always knew I’d go to university, without even knowing what it was; it was predestined, I had to go.”
Lætitia évoque le stress qu’elle ressent: Lætitia recalls the stress she felt as a child when faced with failure. “When I got bad grades, I cried. I was really scared to tell my mother I’d failed an exam. For me, academic validation was something that left its mark.” Lætitia still lives with this pressure her mother placed on academic success. “I feel that pressure: I have to meet the goals my mother set for me, or exceed them, in the best-case scenario.”
Adrianna, la cadette du groupe, est une: Adrianna, the youngest of the group, is a young freelance marketing strategy consultant and esthetician. Unlike the other panellists, she says she benefited from an upbringing that allowed her to discover and express herself without constantly being pushed to excel in every area. “Me, I didn’t have to fight with my parents.” For her, there’s no question of submitting to outside pressure as a Black person. “My parents taught me to be human. I’m not trying to be an excellent Black woman, I’m trying to be Adrianna and excellent, that’s all.”
Elle reconnaît avoir fait l’expérience d: She acknowledges experiencing differential treatment when she worked at a bank. However, she refuses to bend to the expectations of the white majority in order to fit a preconceived image of what a Black woman should “be” or how she should behave.
<strong>« Si je n’avais pas ce fardeau-l: “If I didn’t have that burden, what would I have done with my life?”
Dans la salle, plusieurs sont issus de f: Several people in the room come from immigrant families and, for that reason, experience a double pressure: the pressure to excel as members of the Black community and the pressure to make their parents proud, since their parents immigrated to improve their quality of life.
Paula, étudiante en science politique à: Paula, a political science student at the Université de Montréal, is among those who feel this double pressure. Originally from the Dominican Republic, the young woman immigrated at age 12. “I’ve always been convinced that I didn’t leave my country for nothing. So I felt this responsibility to make something of my life, and I still wonder what I would have done if I hadn’t had that burden.”
Actuellement aux études, Paula admet que: Currently in school, Paula admits that for her parents, going to university is neither an achievement nor a source of pride. “Within my family, I’m not seen as an example of Black excellence; I’m just doing what they think is right,” she says. Then she adds: “I don’t see why I should have to excel in my field to be accepted and loved by the people around me, but I was raised that way, so it’s really hard to shake that off. It’s very hard to imagine that it’s okay to be mediocre at something.”
Cette pression que vivent les personnes: This pressure experienced by members of the Black community affects, among other things, their ability to rest, our guests tell us. “I’m learning to have idle moments; it was mostly the pandemic that forced me to learn how to rest,” Manuel tells us.
Alors que la soirée tire à sa fin, les i: As the evening draws to a close, the participants discuss initiatives that could be put in place so they no longer have to live under the pressure of Black excellence.
Pour Anthony, il est essentiel de célébr: For Anthony, it’s essential to celebrate all forms of Black success, even the most modest: “Every success deserves to be recognized,” he says. “Even a student who passes Secondary 5, that’s Black excellence.” It’s an idea Lætitia shares: “We have to count all our successes. Doing the dishes is Black excellence too!” she says, as the participants laugh.
D’un commun avis, les panélistes insiste: The panellists agree on the importance of communication and connecting with people in the community. “You have to talk to people who are able to understand what you’re feeling,” says Lætitia.
Adrianna conclut cette soirée de dialogu: Adrianna wraps up the evening of dialogue with a big smile and a reminder: “It’s okay to be mediocre, too!”
